newsitem.title: ITALY: New Olivetti head says will sell PCs, other units.
newsitem.headline: New Olivetti head says will sell PCs, other units.

text.p: Olivetti's top manager promised Thursday to sell off a string of businesses, including the money-losing personal computers unit, and to nurse the company back to profit by 1998.

Chief Executive Officer Roberto Colaninno told financial analysts he planned to divest Olivetti's ailing PC business and three other units by the end of this year, raising some 800 billion lire ($526 million).
It was Colaninno's first presentation to the financial community since his appointment last month to replace Francesco Caio, who was forced out of the company within three months of taking the helm.
Olivetti's future is in its telecommunications businesses, Colaninno said, adding that it had "to recover its vocation as an industrial company and make remunerative products."

Investor concerns over the state of the company came to a head when a former director general, Renzo Francesconi, resigned a month ago after casting doubt on the accuracy of the group's first-half results. The company's shares plunged as a result.
Colaninno said that in addition to the troubled PC division, Olivetti planned to sell its Tecnost business, which makes automated teller machines for banks and ticketing systems.
Decision Systems International, a company providing maintenance services for mainframe computers, and a venture capital business, Venture Capital USA, would also be sold by the end of 1996.

Colaninno said further interests would be sold in 1997, raising the total the company plans to raise from divestments in 1996 and 1997 to between 1 trillion ($658 million) and 1.2 trillion lire ($789 million).
"In 1997 we plan to divest non-commercial activities," he said, without elaborating. "The aim is to bring the company to a position where it is not eating up cash in 1997."
Olivetti also intends to go ahead with a planned flotation of its office equipment subsidiary Lexikon on the New York Stock Exchange in 1997.

Colaninno said Olivetti aimed to restore its finances through the sale of assets. He ruled out making a rights issue to shore up the balance sheet. "The priority is the company's financial equilibrium," he told the meeting of financial analysts. "The solution is not through a capital increase, this is a hypothesis which does not arise."
Olivetti's net debt has escalated in recent months, jumping to 2.39 trillion lire ($1.57 billion) at the end of August from 1.26 trillion ($829 million) at the end of June.
Asked when Olivetti might return to profitability, Colaninno replied, "I have not yet established the plan for 1997, which will be a year of transition ... but 1998 will have a positive result."
Analysts said they were impressed by Colaninno's presentation but added that the credibility of Olivetti, which has not turned a profit since 1990, had been severely strained after years of losses.
"It's very early to judge because they have to deliver on all these promises," said one analyst.
